subject: mathematics
question_text: If θ − φ = π/2, then show that the product of the matrix with rows (cos²θ, cosθ sinθ) and (cosθ sinθ, sin²θ) with the matrix with rows (cos²φ, cosφ sinφ) and (cosφ sinφ, sin²φ) is the zero matrix O.

mark_split.label: Use θ − φ = π/2 to write cos θ and sin θ in terms of φ
Rewrite the first matrix entirely in φ
Multiply and show every entry is zero

verification.note: Source: Baby Bullet-Q, Junior Inter Maths-1A (Sri Publishers, Machilipatnam), book p.55 — SAQ chapter 7 Matrices, answer 45. Printed appearances: TS 17 · AP 18. ⚠ THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S — no [N Marks] tags are printed against this answer (the only SAQ in the chapter that carries them is answer 40 on book p.51, printed 1+1+1+1). The 1+1+2 above puts half the marks on the multiplication itself and one mark each on the two trigonometric conversions that make it possible. The book calls this question "What a mixup! Trigonometry in Algebra", and the trigonometry really is where it is won or lost. The book's SAQ chapter header carries ★★★ and reads "4 Marks"; that star is the CHAPTER's rank, not this question's. This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. Paper position: Maths-1A Section B runs Q11-Q17 at 4 marks each, answer any 5 of 7; Q11 is the Matrices slot.

recall_prompt: Say how you would show this product is zero — say what you do with the given angle condition before multiplying anything.

steps.label: Convert θ into φ
steps.margin_note: First mark, and the idea of the whole question. Two different angles cannot be multiplied together usefully — so use the given condition to write everything in ONE angle before touching the matrices.
steps.memory_tip: Two DIFFERENT angles cannot be multiplied usefully — use the condition to write both in one angle.
lines: Given θ − φ = π/2, so θ = π/2 + φ.
sin θ = sin(π/2 + φ) = cos φ

recall.must_convey: That θ = π/2 + φ is used to get cos θ = −sin φ and sin θ = cos φ, so everything can be written in one angle. The minus sign on cos θ must be spoken.
accept: theta equals pi by two plus phi so cos theta is minus sin phi and sin theta is cos phi
use the given condition to convert theta into phi, cos becomes minus sin and sin becomes cos
write theta as ninety degrees plus phi then cos theta is negative sin phi
theta equals pi by two plus phi, appudu cos theta minus sin phi and sin theta cos phi
convert everything to one angle using the allied angle formulas
reject: theta minus phi is pi by two

steps.why: The two matrices are in different angles, and nothing cancels while that is true. Turning θ into φ is what makes every entry comparable — the algebra afterwards is routine.
common_mistakes: Writing cos(π/2 + φ) = sin φ and losing the minus sign, which makes the product non-zero.
Using θ = π/2 − φ instead of π/2 + φ.
Multiplying the matrices first and hoping the condition helps later.

steps.label: Rewrite the first matrix
steps.margin_note: Second mark. cos²θ becomes sin²φ, sin²θ becomes cos²φ, and the off-diagonal cosθ sinθ becomes (−sin φ)(cos φ) — negative. That single minus is what makes the whole product vanish.
steps.memory_tip: cos²θ becomes sin²φ, and the off-diagonal becomes (−sinφ)(cosφ) — that single minus does the work.
lines: cos θ sin θ = (−sin φ)(cos φ) = −sin φ cos φ

recall.must_convey: That the first matrix is rewritten entirely in φ, with the off-diagonal entries becoming NEGATIVE sin φ cos φ.
accept: substitute so the first matrix becomes sin squared phi and minus sin phi cos phi and cos squared phi
rewrite the first matrix in terms of phi with the off diagonal entries negative
replace cos theta by minus sin phi throughout so the corner entries turn negative
first matrix ni phi lo rasi, off diagonal entries minus avthai
convert every entry of the first matrix into phi

steps.why: The diagonal entries swap places — cos² becomes sin² and sin² becomes cos² — and the off-diagonal entries change sign. Both effects are needed for the cancellation, so the substitution has to be done on all four entries.
common_mistakes: Substituting into the diagonal but leaving the off-diagonal entries in θ.
Losing the minus sign on the off-diagonal entries.
Substituting into the SECOND matrix, which is already in φ and must be left alone.

steps.label: Multiply the matrices
steps.margin_note: Half the marks. Multiply row by column. Each entry is a difference of two identical products, so each cancels to zero — write at least two of them out in full to show it is cancellation and not luck.
steps.memory_tip: Each entry is a difference of two identical products, so each cancels to zero.
lines: Entry (1,2):  sin³φ cos φ − sin³φ cos φ = 0
Entry (2,1):  −sin φ cos³φ + sin φ cos³φ = 0

lines.text: ∴ The product is the zero matrix O.

recall.must_convey: That the two matrices are multiplied row against column and every entry is a difference of two equal terms, so all four entries are zero and the product is O.
accept: multiply row by column and each entry is a difference of two identical terms so every entry is zero
the four entries all cancel to zero giving the null matrix
each product entry has two equal terms with opposite signs so it vanishes
row into column multiply cheste prathi entry lo rendu terms cancel ayi zero avthundi
all four entries come to zero so the product is the zero matrix

steps.why: The minus sign introduced in the last step is what makes each pair of terms cancel instead of double. Without it every entry would be twice something rather than zero.
common_mistakes: Writing "= 0" instead of "= O" — the answer is a matrix.
Showing one entry is zero and asserting the other three.
Multiplying entry by entry instead of row by column.

insider_note: Use θ = π/2 + φ to rewrite the FIRST matrix entirely in φ — comparing two different angles directly gets nowhere. cos θ = −sin φ, and that minus sign is what cancels everything.
